conversation.content:
Hello there. I’m so glad we’re getting a chance to talk today. My name is Maya Bennett, and I’m the perinatal mental-health clinician who works with new parents after delivery. I’m here to help you feel heard and supported as you settle into life with your baby.

To guide our conversation, I’ll be using something called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually shortened to the EPDS. It’s a 10-question check-in that looks at how you’ve been feeling physically and emotionally over the past seven days. It isn’t a test you can pass or fail; it simply gives us a snapshot of how things are going for you right now.

Everything we discuss is confidential, and my goal is to create a calm, no-pressure space where you can speak freely. The questions are short, and we’ll take them one at a time. If anything feels uncomfortable, let me know and we can slow down or pause.

Ready to begin?  
Here’s the first question:

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

(soft half-smile)  
I can still laugh—like when my husband made a silly face at 3 a.m. while changing a diaper—but it feels… muted. I’ll chuckle, then it fades fast, almost like I have to remind myself it’s okay to enjoy the moment.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… most of the time I can still laugh, but it feels kind of forced or doesn’t last long. Like, I’ll giggle at something goofy the baby does, but then the smile just slips away and I’m back to feeling flat again.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Sometimes I do—like yesterday I was excited to take the baby for a walk to the park—but the excitement doesn’t feel as big as it used to. It’s more of a quiet “that’ll be nice” than a real spark.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Yesterday the baby was fussy for an hour and I kept thinking, “Maybe my milk isn’t good enough,” or “I must’ve done something to upset him.” I know it’s probably not true, but the thought still pops up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes my heart just races when the baby’s asleep—like I’ll suddenly think, “What if he stops breathing and I don’t notice?” I check the monitor, see his chest moving, and I calm down pretty quick, but those little surges of worry still sneak in for no real reason.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—more like a quick jolt of “what if something bad happens?” and then it passes. I haven’t had a full-blown panic feeling, just those brief worried flashes.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. Like when the laundry pile looks bigger than the baby and I can’t figure out what to tackle first, my chest gets tight and I think, “How am I going to keep up?” But if I break it into tiny steps—fold five onesies, wash three bottles—I can usually push through.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, it’s not that bad. I can still fall asleep once my head hits the pillow. Sometimes it takes me an extra ten or fifteen minutes because my mind keeps replaying the day, but I wouldn’t say I’m lying there miserable or wide-awake all night.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel kind of sad some days—like a heaviness sits on me—but it’s not constant. I’ll tear up for a minute when the baby won’t settle, then I wipe my face and keep going. Most of the time I’m just steady, not happy, not awful, just… flat.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried… maybe twice this week. Once when the baby wouldn’t nap and I felt like I was failing, and once when my mom left after visiting—just felt suddenly alone. It wasn’t all-day sobbing; the tears came, lasted a few minutes, then I wiped my face and kept going.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that. I’ve felt overwhelmed and tired, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 13: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item self-report with follow-up clarification

Symptoms / Concerns
- Anhedonia: diminished ability to enjoy activities; laughter feels “forced” or quickly fades  
- Low/flat mood: reports “heaviness,” intermittent tearfulness (2 crying episodes this week)  
- Excessive self-blame: attributes baby’s fussiness to personal inadequacy (“my milk isn’t good enough”)  
- Worry & anxious arousal: racing heart, intrusive “what-if” thoughts about infant safety; resolves quickly but occurs repeatedly  
- Feeling overwhelmed: chest tightness and task paralysis when facing household duties; improves with step-wise approach  
- Sleep: no difficulty initiating sleep; mild pre-sleep rumination (≤15 min delay)  
- Safety: denies thoughts of self-harm

Pattern
Mood symptoms present most days, fluctuating, without pervasive impairment in functioning or safety risk.

Screening Impression
Signs consistent with mild-to-moderate postpartum depression and comorbid anxiety; does not meet threshold for severe episode. No self-harm ideation. Recommend routine follow-up in 1–2 weeks and formal clinical assessment with standardized tool (EPDS or PHQ-9) to quantify severity and inform next steps.
